doc.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Bands as universities and unspoken communication
summary: Bands where players live and travel together develop chemistry and mutual respect.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you. You know you did study technically, but can you relate to us how you feel like the bands themselves were little universities?

Oh, yeah. Well that’s always, you always try to surround yourself with the best, you know. You always want to play with somebody that’s better than you, and some people are just more compatible than others. I mean they can all be great but they still have to be compatible musically. So when you get you know a situation where the chemistry is right and the people are compatible and they know what they’re doing, and then they bring in you know styles and information and experience from different places, so it works together. And then they have a mutual respect for each other, you know, musically.

Could you relate to us how you know for instance I see bands play and it seems like there’s certain amounts of unspoken communication going on on the stage. I mean all the musicians are competent and they know the changes, but there are special nights, special times during a performance sometimes when unspoken communication takes place.

Well if you catch a band and people that live together, you know, and that’s the way you’re going to have a band. Otherwise you’ve just got a lot of good musicians together. But if people live together and you know they move together and travel together, they, you know, it’s a lot of little inside things that happen, you know and so, that always goes on too you know. But that just comes from being together.
